Weighting each group by its distance sums to the Wiener index 28.0." width="100%"} The Wiener index is the sum of all pairwise shortest path distances in the graph. It is a fundamental topological descriptor used in chemistry and network analysis to measure graph compactness. For undirected graphs: `W(G) = Σ_{u < v} d(u, v)`. For directed graphs: `W(G) = Σ_{u ≠ v} d(u, v)`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, edge weights (`1` where missing) are the distances. If `False`, every edge has distance `1`. If `None` (default), follows whether the graph was created as weighted. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Wiener index. Returns `0.0` for empty graphs or single-node graphs. Returns infinity (`float('inf')`) for disconnected graphs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Wiener index (Wiener, 1947) is the sum of all pairwise shortest-path distances, originally introduced as a topological descriptor for the boiling points of alkanes and now the standard *compactness* metric across chemistry, drug design, and network theory: $W(G) = \sum_{u < v} d(u, v)$ on undirected graphs, or $\sum_{u \ne v}$ on directed ones. The tree case admits a beautiful closed form: for every edge $e$ that splits the tree into subtrees of size $n_1(e)$ and $n_2(e)$, that edge contributes $n_1(e) \cdot n_2(e)$ to the total, so $W(T) = \sum_e n_1(e) \cdot n_2(e)$. Disconnected graphs return $+\infty$ because some pairs have no finite distance. Runtime is $O(V(V + E))$ for unweighted graphs (BFS from every source) and $O(V(V + E) \log V)$ for weighted ones (Dijkstra from every source). ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 4-node path, the Wiener index sums every pairwise distance: `1+2+3+1+2+1 = 10`: ::: {#19981488 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(4) # Returns 10.0 graph.wiener_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10.0 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph has every pair at distance 1, so its Wiener index is simply the number of node pairs, `n*(n-1)/2`; a cycle of similar size has a larger index, since some pairs are farther apart: ::: {#02b44508 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} complete = ec.Graph() complete.add_full_graph(5) cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(6) # Returns (10.0, 18.0) (complete.wiener_index(), cycle.wiener_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (10.0, 27.0) ``` ::: :::
